Thoughts, with the numbers from a first look, since the join can be tested right now without changing anything.

**What the timestamps say today.** The opening commit and its agent-repo pair share the push moment, and the transcript has the push call at that same second:

| Thing | Time (UTC) |
|---|---|
| opening, author | 2026-09-01 21:59:33 (the split that created the working-copy commit) |
| opening, committer | 2026-09-02 00:18:19 (the push) |
| agent-repo pair commit | 2026-09-02 00:18:19 |
| transcript line 462, the push tool call | 2026-09-02 00:18:19.502 |

So the join by time works to the second. One surprise: the pair commit holds transcript lines 1 to 460, and the push call is line 462. The push snapshots the transcript before its own call is appended, so the call that made a pair lives in the *next* pair's slice. The times still bracket it, but "which pair holds the line" is off by one, which a viewer must know.

**What the re-describe will change.** The change id and the author time survive, the committer time becomes the re-describe moment, and the SHA changes. The agent-repo pair keeps the push moment untouched. So after the rewrite the work commit alone no longer knows when it was pushed, only when its rung started. The push moment is still reachable, but through the trailer to the pair, or by searching the transcript for the old title, which is the residue we discussed. That is a real finding about what the trailer carries: not the link, which time gives, but the push moment across a rewrite.

**Line of code to transcript.** The path is `jj file annotate` for the commit, the commit's author and committer times for the slice, and a text search of that slice for the line, which finds the Edit or Bash call that wrote it. I expect it to work for text written by a tool call, and to fail for text written by a script, where the transcript holds the script and not the file. That is worth testing today on a line from the docs rung.

1. Record the before state: the opening's ids and times, the pair's time, lines 445 to 470 of the transcript.

The force-push of the bookmark comes after, under its own approval.

content.text:
Feasible, and the two probes above behave exactly as the method predicts. The chain has four links:

1. **Line to commits.** `jj file annotate` gives the commit that last touched the line, and git's pickaxe on the colocated repo, `git log -S'<text>'`, gives the commit that first introduced it. Both from the work-repo alone.
2. **Commit to transcript slice.** The rung's conversation is the transcript lines its agent-repo pair commit appended. The pair is found by the trailer, or without it by the pair whose time equals the work commit's committer time. One quirk: the push call that made a pair lands in the next pair's slice, so a viewer takes the pair's slice plus the first lines of the next.
3. **Slice to the tool call.** Every edit the agent makes is a tool call whose input holds the text: an Edit's new string, a Write's content, or a Bash script's literal. Search the slice for the line's text and take the first hit.
4. **The decision rule.** If the first hit is a tool call, the agent wrote it, and the assistant text before that call is the why, with your message that opened the turn as the cause. If the first hit is a tool result, the text already existed when the agent first saw it, so a person or a command wrote it. If there is no hit at all, the same. The "verison" line shows this: its first appearance is my read of your edit, and the only tool call holding it is the fix that removed it.

**Where confidence drops:**

- Text the agent produced by transformation, such as a `sed` substitution, holds only a fragment of the line. A substring search still finds it, at lower confidence.
- Generated text, `cargo fmt` output, Cargo.lock, a regenerated config, has no text in the transcript. The attribution is "the agent ran this command", found by the command and its time, not by text.
- The same line written twice in one rung. Take the last call before the push.
- A line the agent wrote in an earlier rung and only moved in this one. Blame names the mover, and the pickaxe finds the writer.

**What history rewrites do to it.** A re-describe or a rebase keeps the change id and the author time and moves only the committer time and SHA, so links 1 and 3 are untouched, and link 2 still holds through the trailer or through the pair's own time. A squash is the one rewrite that breaks it, since the squashed rungs' change ids and pairs vanish, and the rules already bar it for that reason.

So the answer to "did the agent write this line" comes out with high confidence, and "which turn wrote it" comes out at the resolution of one tool call, which is finer than a turn. The error cases are the ones above and are recognizable when they happen.

The plain version: yes. Blame gives the commit, the pair commit gives the conversation slice, a text search of that slice gives the tool call, and the first hit being a call versus a read says whether the agent or a person wrote it.

content.text:
What is established, what is inferred, and what is untested.

**Established by the runs today:**

- The push moment is one second in three places: the work commit's committer time, the pair commit's time, and the transcript line holding the push call. Before any rewrite, time alone joins all three.
- A pair's slice ends just before its own push call. The call that made a pair is the first lines of the next pair's slice. Any viewer must know this.
- A line's author is decided by the type of its first hit in the slice. A tool call means the agent wrote it, a tool result means it already existed when the agent first saw it. Both probes came out right, one Bash script and one hand edit.
- A re-describe keeps the change id, the author time, the trailer, the pair, and the transcript, and moves the SHA and the committer time. Descendants lose their committer times too. So after any rewrite of an ancestor, no work commit on the line knows its push moment. The pair still does.

**Inferred, and I think sound:**

- The author time is the rung's start, since it is when the working-copy commit was created, and it survives rewrites. The rung's pair is then the first pair commit later than that author time. Checked against both rungs: the opening, created by the split at 21:59 UTC, maps to the pair at 00:18, and the docs rung, created at 00:43, maps to the pair at 01:27. So the pair is findable without the trailer even after a rewrite. The trailer is a pointer that skips the search, not the only link.
- The linear agent-repo is what makes "the first pair later than" meaningful. Pairs on branches would need the work commit's line as well. So the journal's linearity is doing quiet work, while the trailer is convenience.

**Untested:**

- The chain end to end from `jj file annotate`, on the landed trapezoid, where the merge commit is a new ancestor of nothing in the transcript.
- Lines from generated files, and lines produced by transformation such as a `sed`, where the text search finds a fragment or nothing.
- The same text written in two rungs, and text that was moved rather than written.
- Whether the first hit rule holds when a Read result and an Edit call share a turn, which is the common case and worked once.

The plain version: a line can be traced to the tool call that wrote it, or shown to be a person's, and a rewrite does not break that because the rung's start time and the change id survive. The trailer is a shortcut, the linear journal is load-bearing, and the landed trapezoid is the case still to run.

content.text:
You are right, and the evidence is now in hand for both points.

**Linearity comes from the transcript.** Its lines are appended with their own timestamps, and the push calls are lines in it too, with the bookmark and title as their text. So the rung boundaries are in the transcript itself, and the join needs the agent-repo only as durable storage for the file, not for its commit structure. What I called the journal's quiet work is really the transcript's. One caveat, measured: the timestamps are not strictly monotonic. This session has 11 backward steps, all attachment or queue lines written a millisecond or two before the message line they belong to. Message lines, user, assistant, tool call and result, are in order among themselves, so a join sorts by timestamp or reads only message lines.

**Compaction appends, it does not rewrite.** Ten earlier sessions in the agent-repo were compacted, and every one shows the same shape: a `user` line flagged `isCompactSummary` sits in the middle of the same file, with hundreds of earlier lines still before it carrying their original timestamps. For example the session from April 24 has the marker at line 622 of 1154, and the first line before it still reads 15:15 on April 24. So compaction changes no timestamp and drops no tool call. What changes is only what the model sees afterward, which does not touch the record of what it did. The one thing to watch is tool calls made after a compaction whose reasoning was in the summarized part. The call is still recorded, but its "why" may live only in the summary line.

The plain version: the transcript is the timeline, the agent-repo just keeps it safe, and compaction adds a summary line without touching what came before, so the code-to-transcript join survives it.

# Code conventions

Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and converges
at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)). Project-local
content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## Line width

Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at the source width in prose.md's
[Line widths](prose.md#line-widths), which matches rustfmt's default `max_width`. The per-commit
flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit applies to the comment text it doesn't
reflow.

## Comments are prose

Doc comments and inline comments are prose and follow prose.md, its
[Semicolons](prose.md#semicolons) rule included: a commit that edits a source file converts that
file's comment semicolons in the same commit, whole file, code spans and the code itself exempt,
using the prose rule's joins (a period, a comma with a conjunction, or a restructure). Files not in
the commit's diff are left alone, since converting them is a sweep and sweeps are their own cycle.

## Doc comments on every file, function, and method

Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have a
`///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough. The discipline is that
the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form)
shape (intro + bullets).

This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to inline `//`
comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected, while inline explanatory comments
inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a non-obvious WHY.

**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows by
default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on any
field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered help.

## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

([why](rationale.md#-ok--comments-on-unwrap-calls-rust))

The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a lean,
not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both in scope:

- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a silently
  substituted value that can hide a wrong result.

When one is used, three obligations attach:

- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are not
    used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and appropriate
  uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects enable the
  project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:

  ```toml
  [lints.clippy]
  unwrap_used = "warn"
  expect_used = "warn"
  ```

  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff, and clippy (in the per-commit flow)
  catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint. They are covered by the
  comment convention and the conversational alert. (The template repository's `CargoRust.toml` seeds
  a base `Cargo.toml` with this section already in place.)

```rust
let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious

match matches.len() {
    1 => {
        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
    }
    // ...
}
```

Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt, since panicking on setup failure is the correct test behavior.

content.text:
Thoughts, and one decision for you at the end.

**The gain is real.** Every listing, `jj status`, GitHub's tree, and an editor's file panel shows the version without opening a file, and the sort-first trick is the same one `!README` uses. Git sorts by bytes, so in `jj` and on GitHub it is first without any locale help.

**The cost is a second copy of the artifact version.** Cargo.toml is the manifest, and versioning.md's rule is that the manifest is the version's only written home, precisely so nothing can drift. A root `!v0.82.0-2` beside `version = "0.82.0-2"` is exactly the drift the rule forbids, unless it is enforced. The fix is cheap here: build.rs already refuses a suffixed version under the stable name on every cargo verb, and it can refuse a root `!v*` entry that does not match `CARGO_PKG_VERSION`, or that has siblings. Then the file is a mirror the build proves, the bump is one more rename in the per-rung Bump step, and the rule gets a sentence saying a guarded mirror is not a second home. For a medium without a manifest, a book or a notes repo, the file *is* the manifest, which is the nicer case.

**Three practical points:**

- An empty file, not a directory. Git does not track empty directories, so the `!v1.2.3` you made is invisible to jj today, harmless, and worth removing before something lands in it.
- In an interactive bash `!v` triggers history expansion, so the name wants quotes when typed. Scripts and jj are unaffected.
- In a locale collation `ls` buries it among the v's, as you saw. Every other tool puts it first.

**Consistency with the set.** If `!vX.Y.Z` means "the version of the directory you are in", the set's file wants the same name: `agent-data/!v0.1.0-2` rather than `agent-data/agent-files-v0.1.0-2`, since the directory already says what is versioned. That makes one convention instead of two, and vc-x1's reader would read `!v*` in `agent-data`. The set file's name is still a draft on this bookmark, so switching costs a content amend in this rung plus the docs rung's text, no re-describe. It is the one thing worth deciding before this cycle closes, because the family will copy whatever name lands.

The root mirror itself is its own cycle: it touches build.rs and a rule, and the per-rung flow.

The plain version: good idea, do it as a build-guarded mirror in its own cycle, use an empty file, and decide now whether the set's file becomes `agent-data/!v0.1.0` so both follow one rule.

content.text:
Three things about that.

**The D plus A is jj's, not the file's.** jj does no rename detection in `jj st`, so every rename shows as a delete and an add there, whatever the content. Git does detect it, and for an empty file the match is exact: the pushed docs rung shows the bump as `R100 agent-data/version-0.1.0-0 → agent-data/agent-files-v0.1.0-1` in `git log --name-status -M`. So history records it as the rename it is, and only the working-copy view reads oddly. A one-line file would show as a single `M` in jj, at the price of the listing visibility, which is the trade already made.

**An untracked empty directory cannot be the record.** Git tracks no empty directory, so it would never be in a commit, and the question the version file answers is "which version at this commit". It would also drift, since nothing bumps or checks it. As a local reminder it is a sticky note, and a wrong one after the first missed rename.

**The sort position in terminals** is the locale's doing, and `LC_COLLATE=C` fixes it for anyone who cares. jj, git, GitHub, and editors sort by bytes, so `!v` is first everywhere but a localized `ls`.

The plain version: the delete-and-add is only how jj displays a rename, git stores it as one, and an untracked directory would be a note rather than a record.

Yes, I think it is right, for three reasons.

**The banner is provenance.** It exists so any captured output says which binary produced it. Which set the run was under is the same kind of fact, and now every stderr capture inside a workspace carries both. That is the case the feature is for.

**Silence outside is the honest form.** Outside a workspace there is nothing to report, and a `(agent-files none)` on every run in `~` would be noise that trains the eye to skip the parenthetical. The report and the subcommand keep the reason for anyone who asks.

**The stable part stays stable.** The first two tokens, name and version, never change, so a script reading `-V` still gets them, and one that wants the set version has `agent-files version` with the bare name. Help never carries the suffix, so its text is the same from any directory.

One thing to watch, not a flaw: the parenthetical moves with the cwd inside nested workspaces, since the root finder stops at the first config it meets walking up. That is what "the workspace you are in" should mean, and the smoke test pins it.

The plain version: good idea, because the banner's job is to say what produced the output, and inside a workspace the set is part of that.

content.text:
Good idea, and bigger than it looks, so I would not fold it into this rung.

**What `-R` is today.** Seven subcommands declare their own `-R`, each with its own default and meaning: `.` for squash-push and the desc pair, optional for validate and sync, and one inside the shared common args. There is no global `-R`, and the root finder is anchored on the cwd, which is why `version` and `-V` cannot take one.

**What it should become.** One global `-R <path>` on the root command, as jj has it, that anchors the workspace root search for every subcommand, `version`, `-V`, and the `agent-files` group included, with the per-subcommand flags retired or made aliases of it. Then `vc-x1 version -R vc-x1` from the parent directory reports that workspace, and the banner follows it too, which is the right reading of "the workspace the run is about".

**Why not now.** Consolidating seven flags into one global changes every command's surface at once, and that is a cycle of its own, not a line in a feature rung about reporting. It pairs naturally with the nesting of the validate commands already in the Todo, since both are CLI-surface consolidation. A `-R` only on `version` would be an eighth local flag, the thing the consolidation exists to remove.

So my suggestion is a Todo entry, "Global -R anchors the workspace for every command", ranked with the nesting entry, and this rung pushes as reviewed.

The plain version: yes to `-R` on version and the banner, as one global flag for every command, in its own cycle rather than this rung.
